title: Studying electron beam coherence using plasmon interference
authors: Evelijn Akerboom, F. Javier García de Abajo, Albert Polman
abstract: Energetic electrons create distinct cathodoluminescence (CL) angular distributions upon interaction with dielectric and plasmonic nanostructures, providing valuable information on coherences in the excitation pathways. A counterintuitive prediction is that the CL signals arising from the excitation associated with different lateral regions of an extended electron wave are mutually incoherent and do not interfere, while the signals originating from different structures within the electromagnetic field of a narrow electron beam are mutually coherent. We present conclusive experimental evidence of these effects by examining the angular CL emission profile from defocused electron-beam excitation of a thin silicon nitride film, which is shown to follow an incoherent sum of CL excitations within the electron beam spot. In contrast, CL interferences are observed for separated plasmonic scatterers excited within the evanescent field of a single electron. Coherence may be recovered through correlations between emitted light and post-selected electron states, for which we propose a measurement geometry that erases which-path information of the electron trajectory.
summary: The research uses cathodoluminescence from plasmonic nanostructures to probe electron beam coherence. It experimentally demonstrates that while single electrons passing sequentially through multiple scatterers exhibit clear interference patterns, using a broad electron beam averages over these paths, resulting only in an incoherent sum. The work highlights the critical role of preserving quantum path information for observing coherent quantum effects.
main_problem: The study investigates how electron beam coherence affects cathodoluminescence (CL) signals when exciting plasmonic nanostructures, specifically comparing interference effects from single-electron paths versus extended beam excitation.
main_result: Interference patterns are observed when the electron passes coherently through multiple separated plasmonic scatterers within the evanescent field; however, these interferences are lost when using a widely defocused (extended) electron beam spot.
method: Angle-resolved cathodoluminescence (AR CL) measurements were performed on thin films and double plasmonic pillars using scanning electron microscopes, complemented by Fourier transform analysis of spectral data.
model_or_system: The experiments use energetic electrons exciting $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ films or gold-coated nanopillars. The theoretical framework contrasts the incoherent sum expected from extended beams with the coherent interference observed when path information is preserved (e.g., passing between pillars).
key_observables: Angular CL emission profile, $	ext{k}_\parallel$-space images showing interference fringes, and time-of-flight components derived from Fourier transforms.
important_parameters: Electron beam spot size ($\sim 4 	ext{ nm}$ vs. $\mu	ext{m}$), plasmonic pillar separation, and the ability to correlate CL emission with post-selected electron states.
main_assumptions: The nonrecoil approximation is used in theoretical calculations; a key limitation noted is that extended beams inherently erase which-path information necessary for observing interference.
figures_summary: Figures show AR CL data comparing focused vs. spread beam excitation (incoherent sum); they also display complex interference patterns and Fourier transforms from double plasmonic pillars, identifying components related to pillar heights.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the contrast between incoherent summation over extended beams (using thin films) and coherent interference observed with single-electron paths (using separated scatterers). It then details measurements on double pillars, confirming coherence via TOF analysis, and concludes by proposing correlation measurements to fully retrieve path-dependent interference.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum optics/coherence concepts into solid-state excitation physics using electron beams. The necessity of erasing which-path information echoes fundamental principles in quantum measurement theory, making it relevant for understanding coherence limits in nanoscale spectroscopy.
